t: Difference of Number of Distinct Values on Diagonals
o: For each cell, count distinct values strictly above-left on its ↘ diagonal and strictly below-right, and output the absolute difference. Cells on the same ↘ diagonal share the key r − c. Naively recomputing sets per cell is O((mn)²); better, process each diagonal as a sequence and maintain running sets forward (for leftAbove) and backward (for rightBelow). Constraints (50×50) make even brute force acceptable, but the linear-in-diagonal-length method is clean. Example 1 confirms boundary cells have one side empty (count 0).
k: Cells on a ↘ diagonal share key r − c.
Two passes per diagonal (forward/backward) with incremental sets give both counts.
Boundary cells naturally get 0 on the empty side.

a.i: Group cells by r − c. Walking a diagonal forward, add each cell's value to a set after recording the current set size as its leftAbove. Walking backward similarly yields rightBelow. Each value insertion is O(1) amortized, so total work is linear in matrix size times set operations.
s: Bucket all (r,c) by key r − c.
Forward pass per bucket: record set size, then insert grid[r][c].
Backward pass per bucket: record set size as rightBelow, then insert.
a.t: O(mn) — each cell inserted into sets a constant number of times
a.sp: O(mn) for buckets, sets, and output

a.i: For each cell, walk up-left collecting a set and down-right collecting another set. O(mn·min(m,n)) time — perfectly fine for 50×50 and easiest to reason about.
s: For each (r,c): walk (r−1,c−1), (r−2,c−2)... into set A.
a.t: O(mn·min(m,n)) — each cell scans its diagonal halves

w: Give brute force first, then the diagonal-bucketed version as the scalable answer. Pitfalls: excluding the cell itself from both sides, diagonal key choice (r − c vs c − r — either works if consistent), and remembering diagonals starting in the last row/column. Follow-up: extend to anti-diagonals (key r + c) or count distinct values with updates (would need persistent structures).
